Customers link to a state/province through their delivery city: Sales.Customers.DeliveryCityID → Application.Cities.CityID → Application.StateProvinces.StateProvinceID. I'll join those tables and count customers per StateProvinceName.

```sql
SELECT sp.StateProvinceName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.StateProvinceName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.StateProvinceName;
```

The "account name" is most likely the customer name, and the account opening date is `AccountOpenedDate` in `Sales.Customers`. I'll order by that date ascending and take one row. I'll add `CustomerID` as a tiebreaker so the result is deterministic when several accounts share the earliest date.

```sql
SELECT CustomerName
FROM Sales.Customers
ORDER BY AccountOpenedDate ASC, CustomerID ASC
LIMIT 1;
```

Average transaction amount per customer: group Sales.CustomerTransactions by CustomerID and average TransactionAmount. I'll join to Customers to include the name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Average quantity sold per stock item: I'll use Sales.InvoiceLines (actual sold quantities), group by stock item, and join to StockItems for the name.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       AVG(il.Quantity) AS average_quantity_sold
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY si.StockItemID;
```

The question doesn't name a table, so I assumed the customer transactions in `Sales.CustomerTransactions`. I also read "completed successfully" as `IsFinalized = true`, since a finalized transaction is fully settled. The query averages `TransactionAmount` over those rows.

```sql
SELECT AVG(TransactionAmount) AS average_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
WHERE IsFinalized = true;
```

Backorders are identified in Sales.Orders by a non-null BackorderOrderID, which links an order to the backorder created for it. Counting the distinct CustomerIDs on those orders gives the number of customers who had backorders.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL;
```

The query assumes Black Friday 2024 is 2024-11-29, the day after US Thanksgiving. I count an order as "with promotion" if any of its lines matches a special deal active on that date. A deal matches only when every non-null criterion (stock item, stock group, customer, buying group, customer category) fits the order line. Order value is the sum of quantity × unit price across its lines. The query returns the average of that value for each group.

```sql
WITH bf_orders AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           o.OrderDate,
           c.BuyingGroupID,
           c.CustomerCategoryID
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
    WHERE o.OrderDate = DATE '2024-11-29'
),
order_values AS (
    SELECT b.OrderID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value,
           BOOL_OR(EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM Sales.SpecialDeals d
               WHERE b.OrderDate BETWEEN d.StartDate AND d.EndDate
                 AND (d.StockItemID IS NULL OR d.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
                 AND (d.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                        SELECT 1
                        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sg
                        WHERE sg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
                          AND sg.StockGroupID = d.StockGroupID))
                 AND (d.CustomerID IS NULL OR d.CustomerID = b.CustomerID)
                 AND (d.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR d.BuyingGroupID = b.BuyingGroupID)
                 AND (d.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR d.CustomerCategoryID = b.CustomerCategoryID)
           )) AS has_promotion
    FROM bf_orders b
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = b.OrderID
    GROUP BY b.OrderID
)
SELECT has_promotion,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_value), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM order_values
GROUP BY has_promotion
ORDER BY has_promotion DESC;
```

Revenue is best taken from invoice lines: the sum of ExtendedPrice for invoices dated in Q1 2013 (January 1 to March 31, 2013). Credit notes are rare in this dataset, and ExtendedPrice already includes tax. Revenue is usually net of tax, so I'll compute it as ExtendedPrice minus TaxAmount, which equals Quantity * UnitPrice.

Alternatively, I could use CustomerTransactions.AmountExcludingTax, but that also includes payments and so isn't a pure revenue measure. Invoice lines are the cleaner source.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2013-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2013-04-01';
```

"Stock count" is ambiguous. It could mean the number of stock items per brand, or total quantity on hand. I'll go with total quantity on hand from StockItemHoldings, since that's the actual stock held. Brand is nullable, so I'll exclude nulls.

Steps:
1. Join StockItems to StockItemHoldings on StockItemID.
2. Group by Brand and sum QuantityOnHand.
3. Order descending and limit to 10.

```sql
SELECT si.Brand, SUM(h.QuantityOnHand) AS total_stock
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings h ON h.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE si.Brand IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY si.Brand
ORDER BY total_stock DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Sales.Orders has an OrderDate column of type date, so I filter on it for 1 November 2013 and return every column of the matching orders.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = DATE '2013-11-01'
ORDER BY OrderID;
```

Approach: find stock items with Brand 'Northwind', join to invoice lines and invoices, group by customer, and rank by total quantity purchased (the biggest consumer by volume). Customers are taken from Invoices.CustomerID.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE si.Brand = 'Northwind'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Backorders are identified by `Sales.Orders.BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL`. Each year comes from `OrderDate`, restricted to 2000–2020. The query counts distinct customers per year, and years with no backorders don't appear in the output.

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM OrderDate)::int AS order_year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
  AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM OrderDate) BETWEEN 2000 AND 2020
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year;
```

Order value = sum of OrderLines Quantity * UnitPrice per order. First compute the value per order, then average across orders grouped by customer category.

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
)
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       AVG(ot.order_value) AS average_order_value
FROM order_totals ot
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ot.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.CustomerCategories cc ON cc.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY average_order_value DESC;
```

Delay is the gap between the expected delivery date (Sales.Orders.ExpectedDeliveryDate) and the actual confirmed delivery time (Sales.Invoices.ConfirmedDeliveryTime). The path is Invoices → Orders (for the expected date) and Invoices → Customers (for the delivery city) → Cities.

I'll compute the average delay per city, in days, and keep only invoices that have a confirmed delivery time. Cities are ranked by average delay, highest first, and limited to 5. Grouping by CityID as well as CityName avoids merging distinct cities that share a name.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName,
       AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime - o.ExpectedDeliveryDate::timestamp)) / 86400.0) AS avg_delay_days
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = i.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers cu ON cu.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities c ON c.CityID = cu.DeliveryCityID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY avg_delay_days DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Interpretation: the ratio of salespeople to employees in Application.People, computed as the count of rows with IsSalesperson divided by the count of rows with IsEmployee. A cast to numeric avoids integer division, and NULLIF guards against dividing by zero.

```sql
SELECT
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsSalesperson)::numeric
  / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsEmployee), 0) AS salesperson_to_employee_ratio
FROM Application.People;
```

The schema has no explicit discount column on invoices or order lines. I treated a purchase as discounted when an invoice line's `UnitPrice` is below the stock item's list `UnitPrice`. The query counts distinct customers with at least one such line on an invoice dated in 2024.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT i.CustomerID) AS customers_with_discount
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2025-01-01'
  AND il.UnitPrice < si.UnitPrice;
```

Stock items are in Warehouse.StockItems, which has both Size and UnitPrice columns. Grouping by Size and averaging UnitPrice gives the answer.

```sql
SELECT Size, AVG(UnitPrice) AS average_unit_price
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
GROUP BY Size;
```

Vehicles appear only in `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, identified by `VehicleRegistration`. The number of vehicles is the count of distinct registrations in that table.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VehicleRegistration) AS vehicle_count
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures;
```

Every item in `Warehouse.StockItems` has a `TaxRate` column defined as `NOT NULL`, so I read "no tax rate attached" as `TaxRate IS NULL`. Because of the constraint, this should return 0.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items_without_tax_rate
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE TaxRate IS NULL;
```

Interpretation: "items sold" is the total quantity sold on invoice lines, linked to suppliers through each stock item's supplier.

Steps:
1. Join `Sales.InvoiceLines` to `Warehouse.StockItems` on `StockItemID`.
2. Join to `Purchasing.Suppliers` on `SupplierID`.
3. Sum `Quantity` per supplier, sort descending, and keep the top 5.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = si.SupplierID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_items_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Suppliers link to cities through DeliveryCityID (the city used in the Website.Suppliers view), so I join Purchasing.Suppliers to Application.Cities on that column. I group by CityID and CityName, since city names may repeat across states. Then I count suppliers per city, sort descending, and keep the top 5.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName, COUNT(*) AS supplier_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Application.Cities c ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY supplier_count DESC, c.CityName
LIMIT 5;
```

Interpretation: for each city that has suppliers (using the delivery city), compute population divided by the number of suppliers in it, and return the top 5 highest ratios.

Steps:
1. Join Purchasing.Suppliers to Application.Cities on DeliveryCityID.
2. Group by city and count the suppliers.
3. Divide LatestRecordedPopulation by the supplier count.
4. Order descending and limit to 5.

```sql
SELECT c.CityID,
       c.CityName,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation,
       COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS supplier_count,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation::numeric / COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS population_to_supplier_ratio
FROM Application.Cities c
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE c.LatestRecordedPopulation IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName, c.LatestRecordedPopulation
ORDER BY population_to_supplier_ratio DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Nothing in the schema logs actual user searches. The closest thing to search terms is the `Tags` column on `Warehouse.StockItems`, which holds a JSON array of tags per item. The query unnests each array and counts how many stock items carry each tag, then returns the 6 most common.

```sql
SELECT tag AS search_term,
       COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(si.Tags::jsonb) AS tag
WHERE si.Tags IS NOT NULL
  AND si.Tags <> ''
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY item_count DESC, search_term
LIMIT 6;
```

Interpreting "geographical area a company targets" as the sales territory, I counted customers per territory and kept the top 3. The path is Sales.Customers → Application.Cities (delivery city) → Application.StateProvinces (SalesTerritory).

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY customer_count DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Interpretation: "items ordered" means the total quantity across order lines, summed per order date. The day with the highest total is the answer.

Steps:
1. Join Sales.Orders to Sales.OrderLines on OrderID.
2. Group by OrderDate and sum Quantity.
3. Order descending and take the top row.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderDate, SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_items
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.OrderDate
ORDER BY total_items DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Approach: I read "best sellers" as the stock items with the highest total quantity sold on invoice lines. I limited the sales to customers whose delivery city is in a country on the continent "North America". This is reached through city, state/province and country. I rank by total quantity and take the top 4.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
JOIN Application.Countries co ON co.CountryID = sp.CountryID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE co.Continent = 'North America'
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC
LIMIT 4;
```

The question doesn't define "successful", so I took it to mean the special deal with the highest total sales revenue. The query matches each deal to invoice lines that fall inside its date range and satisfy its criteria. A NULL criterion on a deal matches anything. The criteria are stock item, customer, buying group, customer category and stock group. It sums `ExtendedPrice` per deal and returns the top one. I haven't run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_revenue,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity,
       COUNT(*) AS line_count
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
JOIN Sales.Invoices i
  ON i.InvoiceDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR i.CustomerID = sd.CustomerID)
JOIN Sales.Customers c
  ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR c.BuyingGroupID = sd.BuyingGroupID)
 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR c.CustomerCategoryID = sd.CustomerCategoryID)
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il
  ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR il.StockItemID = sd.StockItemID)
 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
GROUP BY sd.SpecialDealID, sd.DealDescription
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

I took "sale transactions" to mean rows in `Sales.CustomerTransactions`, counted per calendar month (year and month together). The query orders the months by that count and returns the top one. I did not filter by transaction type, so payments and credit notes are included in the count.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS transaction_count
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)
ORDER BY transaction_count DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Customers who placed more than 130 orders: join Sales.Orders to Sales.Customers, group by customer, and keep groups with a count above 130.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
HAVING COUNT(o.OrderID) > 130
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

The Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures table holds the cold room readings, with the timestamp in RecordedWhen and the value in Temperature. I'll select those two columns and order by time.

```sql
SELECT RecordedWhen, Temperature
FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
ORDER BY RecordedWhen;
```

Orders link to customers via CustomerID, and customers link to buying groups via BuyingGroupID. Joining Orders to Customers, then to BuyingGroups, and grouping by buying group gives the order count for each one. I use inner joins so only customers that belong to a buying group are counted, since orders from customers without one have no group to report.

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupID,
       bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.BuyingGroups bg
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.BuyingGroupID = bg.BuyingGroupID
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY bg.BuyingGroupName;
```

The question doesn't say which table holds "purchases", so I assumed purchase orders. The query sums ordered quantity × expected unit price per outer for each supplier, over orders dated in 2014. I haven't run it against the data.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(pol.OrderedOuters * pol.ExpectedUnitPricePerOuter) AS total_purchases_2014
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrders po
JOIN Purchasing.PurchaseOrderLines pol ON pol.PurchaseOrderID = po.PurchaseOrderID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = po.SupplierID
WHERE po.OrderDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
  AND po.OrderDate < DATE '2015-01-01'
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_purchases_2014 DESC;
```

Invoices are in Sales.Invoices, and InvoiceDate is a date column. I filter it to the half-open range from 2014-05-01 up to but not including 2014-06-01, which covers all of May 2014. The query returns InvoiceID, CustomerID, and InvoiceDate.

```sql
SELECT InvoiceID, CustomerID, InvoiceDate
FROM Sales.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-05-01'
  AND InvoiceDate < DATE '2014-06-01'
ORDER BY InvoiceDate, InvoiceID;
```

"Order details with customer names" most plausibly means order lines joined to their orders and customers. So I join Sales.Orders to Sales.Customers for the customer name, then to Sales.OrderLines for the line details.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.ExpectedDeliveryDate,
       c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen
FROM Sales.Orders AS o
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines AS ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Approach: The question asks for a monthly summary, but also says "grouped by invoice date". Sales.Invoices has TotalDryItems and TotalChillerItems, so I'll truncate InvoiceDate to the month, sum both columns, and also give their combined total.

```sql
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)::date AS invoice_month,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems) AS total_chiller_items,
    SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_dry_items,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems + TotalDryItems) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.Invoices
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY invoice_month;
```

The question asks for the total discount amount for each deal description. The `Sales.SpecialDeals` table holds `DealDescription` and `DiscountAmount`, so I group by the description and sum the discount amount.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription, SUM(DiscountAmount) AS TotalDiscountAmount
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
GROUP BY DealDescription;
```

Step by step:

1. The table `Sales.CustomerTransactions` holds each customer's transactions.
2. `TransactionAmount` is the total including tax (AmountExcludingTax + TaxAmount), so it is the right column for "transaction amount including tax".
3. Group by customer and average `TransactionAmount`. I join to `Sales.Customers` to include the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount_including_tax
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Approach: sum `TransactionAmount` per customer from `Sales.CustomerTransactions`, join to `Sales.Customers` for the name, order by the total descending, and keep the top 100.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS TotalTransactionAmount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY TotalTransactionAmount DESC
LIMIT 100;
```

Join Purchasing.SupplierTransactions to Purchasing.Suppliers on SupplierID. Every transaction has a SupplierID that is NOT NULL and a foreign key to Suppliers, so an inner join keeps all transactions and adds each supplier's name.

```sql
SELECT st.*, s.SupplierName
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions AS st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers AS s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
ORDER BY st.SupplierTransactionID;
```

Order details are the rows in Sales.OrderLines. Each row carries a StockItemID, so joining to Warehouse.StockItems on that column gives the stock item name.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen,
       ol.LastEditedBy,
       ol.LastEditedWhen
FROM Sales.OrderLines AS ol
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems AS si ON si.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "order details with special deals" as order lines whose order matches a special deal. A deal applies when the order date falls within the deal's start and end dates. Each of the deal's optional criteria (stock item, customer, buying group, customer category, stock group) must either be null or match the order. I haven't run the query.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.CustomerID,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       sd.DiscountAmount,
       sd.DiscountPercentage,
       sd.UnitPrice AS DealUnitPrice
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID, sd.SpecialDealID;
```
